q: A rare disorder damages the efferent fibers of the autonomic nervous system while sparing all other nerve fibers. Which function would be directly affected?
o: Changes in heart rate during exercise
Sensing stretch of a full stomach wall
Voluntary flexing of the elbow joint
Detection of pain from the skin of the hand
w: Autonomic efferent (motor) fibers control cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands, so adjusting the heart rate would be lost. Sensory (afferent) fibers and somatic motor fibers are spared.

n.1: Sensing stretch is a sensory (afferent) function; the afferent fibers are spared.
n.2: Flexing the elbow uses skeletal muscle, which is controlled by somatic motor fibers that are spared.
n.3: Pain detection travels on afferent (sensory) fibers, which are spared.

q: Autonomic motor fibers leave the spinal cord between vertebral levels T1 and L2. Which division do these fibers belong to, and what is one effect they produce?
o: Sympathetic; they slow digestion and urination
Parasympathetic; they stimulate digestion and urination
Parasympathetic; they slow the heart rate
w: Two steps: outflow from T1 to L2 is the thoracolumbar, or sympathetic, division. Sympathetic effects include slowing digestion and urination, as well as dilating the bronchioles and pupils and raising the heart rate.

n.1: Stimulating digestion and urination is parasympathetic, and parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral, not thoracolumbar.
n.2: Slowing the heart is a parasympathetic effect, but parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral, not T1 to L2.
n.3: The division is right, but sympathetic stimulation dilates the bronchioles; constriction is parasympathetic.

q: At the target organs they control, the two autonomic divisions mainly release different neurotransmitters. Which pair lists the main parasympathetic neurotransmitter first and the main sympathetic neurotransmitter second?
w: Parasympathetic neurons release acetylcholine at their target organs. The main sympathetic effector neurotransmitter is norepinephrine.

n.1: Acetylcholine is the parasympathetic transmitter; the sympathetic division mainly releases norepinephrine at its targets.
n.2: Epinephrine is mainly a hormone released into the blood by the adrenal medulla; sympathetic nerve endings mainly release norepinephrine.
n.3: This reverses the two divisions: acetylcholine is parasympathetic and norepinephrine is sympathetic.

q: A hiker rounds a bend and nearly steps on a rattlesnake. Which combination of changes would his autonomic nervous system most likely produce in the next few seconds?
o: Faster heart rate, dilated pupils and increased digestion
Faster heart rate, constricted pupils and slowed digestion
Slower heart rate, dilated pupils and increased digestion
Faster heart rate, dilated pupils and slowed digestion
w: A sudden threat triggers the sympathetic (fight or flight) division, which increases the heart rate, dilates the pupils and slows digestion at the same time.

n.0: Sympathetic stimulation slows digestion; increased digestion is a parasympathetic (rest and digest) effect.
n.1: Constricted pupils are a parasympathetic effect; sympathetic stimulation dilates them.
n.2: A slower heart rate and increased digestion are parasympathetic effects; the sympathetic response speeds the heart and slows digestion.

q: Stretch receptors in the bladder wall signal that the bladder is full. The signal travels to the spinal cord, and the reply makes the smooth muscle of the bladder wall contract. Which fibers carried the incoming and outgoing signals?
o: Afferent fibers in; somatic motor fibers out
Afferent fibers in; sympathetic fibers out
Afferent fibers in; parasympathetic fibers out
Efferent fibers in; parasympathetic fibers out
w: Two steps: incoming sensory signals travel on afferent fibers, and contraction of the bladder's smooth muscle to promote urination is a parasympathetic (autonomic motor) effect.

n.0: Somatic motor fibers control skeletal muscle; the bladder wall is smooth muscle under autonomic control.
n.1: The sympathetic division slows urination; the parasympathetic division contracts the bladder wall.
n.3: Signals entering the CNS travel on afferent fibers; efferent fibers carry commands out.

q: When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, which ion flows in and directly triggers the release of neurotransmitter?
w: At the axon terminal, voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open. Ca²⁺ entry makes synaptic vesicles fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis.

n.0: Na⁺ entry drives depolarization along the axon, but the trigger for vesicle release at the terminal is Ca²⁺.
n.1: K⁺ flows out of the neuron during repolarization; it does not trigger neurotransmitter release.
n.3: Cl⁻ entry tends to inhibit a neuron, as when GABA binds its receptors; it does not trigger release from the terminal.

q: A biopsy of the sciatic nerve, which is part of the peripheral nervous system, shows myelinated axons. Which cells produced the myelin sheath around these axons?
w: In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is made by Schwann cells. In the central nervous system, oligodendrocytes make it.

n.0: Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the CNS, not in peripheral nerves such as the sciatic nerve.
n.2: Satellite cells are PNS glia that surround cell bodies in ganglia; Schwann cells form PNS myelin.
n.3: Astrocytes are CNS glia that support neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier; they do not make myelin.

q: At rest, the inside of a typical neuron is about -70 mV relative to the outside. Which mechanism uses ATP directly to help maintain this resting membrane potential?
o: Na⁺/K⁺ pump moving 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels letting Na⁺ flow in
Ca²⁺ channels letting Ca²⁺ into the axon terminal
Na⁺/K⁺ pump moving 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in
w: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in. Together with K⁺ leak channels, this keeps the inside of the resting neuron negative.

n.1: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open at threshold and cause depolarization; they are passive channels, not an ATP-driven pump.
n.2: Ca²⁺ channels at the axon terminal open during synaptic transmission; they do not maintain the resting potential.
n.3: The ratio is reversed: the pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in.

q: When a stimulus brings a neuron's membrane to threshold, the membrane rapidly depolarizes. Which ion movement is directly responsible for this depolarization?
o: Na⁺ being pumped out of the cell
K⁺ flowing out of the cell
w: At threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes into the cell, making the inside less negative (depolarization).

n.0: Pumping Na⁺ out is the work of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, which maintains the resting potential rather than depolarizing the membrane.
n.2: K⁺ flowing out of the cell causes repolarization, the phase after depolarization.
n.3: K⁺ does not cause depolarization by entering; Na⁺ entry depolarizes the membrane.

q: Two axons have the same diameter, but one is myelinated and the other is not. Why does an impulse travel faster along the myelinated axon?
o: Myelin carries the impulse in place of the axon membrane
The impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next
Myelin increases the size of each action potential
Myelin releases neurotransmitter along the axon's length
w: Myelin insulates the axon, so the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier (gap in the myelin) to the next. This saltatory conduction is faster than continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon.

n.0: Myelin is insulation; the action potential is still generated by the axon membrane at the nodes of Ranvier.
n.2: Action potentials are all-or-none; myelin speeds conduction but does not make each action potential larger.
n.3: Neurotransmitter is released from axon terminals at the synapse, not by myelin along the axon.

q: A researcher stimulates a neuron with a stimulus well above threshold and then with a stimulus twice as strong. How does the neuron's response to the stronger stimulus differ?
o: Action potentials fire more often; each is the same size
Each action potential is about twice as large
Action potentials keep the same rate, but each one lasts longer
Each action potential travels about twice as fast
w: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached, each one is the same size. A stronger stimulus increases how often action potentials fire, not their size.

n.1: Action potentials are all-or-none, so a stronger stimulus does not make each one larger.
n.2: Stimulus strength is coded by firing frequency; the rate rises rather than staying the same.
n.3: Conduction speed depends on the axon itself, such as whether it is myelinated, not on stimulus strength.

q: At the junction between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber, a neurotransmitter triggers contraction and is then broken down by an enzyme in the synaptic cleft. Which neurotransmitter is it?
w: At the neuromuscular junction, motor neurons release acetylcholine, which is broken down in the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase.

n.1: Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter of the CNS, not the transmitter released onto skeletal muscle.
n.2: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter of the brain, not the one released at the neuromuscular junction.
n.3: Norepinephrine is the main sympathetic effector neurotransmitter, not the transmitter at the neuromuscular junction.

q: Which glial cells of the central nervous system wrap brain capillaries with their processes and help form the blood-brain barrier?
w: Astrocytes are star-shaped CNS glia that support neurons and, with their processes on brain capillaries, help form the blood-brain barrier.

n.0: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and help make cerebrospinal fluid.
n.1: Microglia are the phagocytes of the CNS; they do not form the blood-brain barrier.
n.2: Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the CNS.

q: A toxin blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels in a neuron while Na⁺ channels continue to work normally. Which phase of the action potential would be most directly impaired?
o: Ca²⁺ entry at the axon terminal
w: Two steps: depolarization depends on Na⁺ entering through Na⁺ channels, while repolarization depends on K⁺ leaving through voltage-gated K⁺ channels. Blocking the K⁺ channels therefore impairs repolarization.

n.1: Depolarization is caused by Na⁺ entering through Na⁺ channels, which still work normally.
n.2: Ca²⁺ enters the axon terminal through Ca²⁺ channels, not K⁺ channels.
n.3: Threshold is reached as the stimulus opens Na⁺ channels; it does not depend on voltage-gated K⁺ channels.

q: After a fall, Diego has damage confined to his cerebellum. Which problem is he most likely to show during his recovery?
o: Loss of control of breathing rhythm
Loss of balance and poorly coordinated movement
Inability to regulate body temperature and thirst
w: The cerebellum coordinates movement and controls balance and posture, so damage to it produces unsteady, poorly coordinated movement.

n.0: Breathing rhythm is set by the medulla oblongata, with help from the pons, not the cerebellum.
n.1: Understanding spoken language depends on Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe.
n.3: Body temperature and thirst are regulated by the hypothalamus.

q: A drug overdose depresses the brain region containing the vital centers that set heart rate, breathing rhythm and blood pressure. Which region is this?
w: The medulla oblongata of the brainstem contains the vital centers for heart rate, breathing rhythm and blood pressure, as well as reflexes such as coughing and swallowing.

n.0: The primary motor cortex in the frontal lobe controls voluntary movement, not heart rate or breathing rhythm.
n.1: The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst and water balance; the vital centers are in the medulla oblongata.
n.2: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and posture; it does not contain the vital centers.

q: During surgery on the spinal cord, the surgeon separates the protective membranes one at a time. Which meningeal layer lies directly against the surface of the spinal cord?
w: From outer to inner, the meninges are the dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater. The pia mater is the innermost layer, lying directly on the brain and spinal cord.

n.1: The arachnoid mater is the middle layer; the subarachnoid space beneath it holds cerebrospinal fluid.
n.2: The dura mater is the outermost, toughest meningeal layer.
n.3: The choroid plexus makes cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles; it is not one of the meninges.

q: After a stroke, a patient cannot feel touch or temperature on his right hand, yet he can still move the hand normally. Which lobe is most likely damaged?
w: The parietal lobe holds the somatosensory cortex, which perceives touch, pain, temperature and body position. Voluntary movement is controlled by the frontal lobe's primary motor cortex, which is spared here.

n.1: The occipital lobe processes vision, not touch or temperature.
n.2: The temporal lobe processes hearing and language comprehension, not touch.
n.3: The frontal lobe's primary motor cortex controls voluntary movement, which is intact in this patient.

q: After a stroke, Mr. Okafor understands questions but struggles to produce fluent speech. Damage to which area, in which lobe, best explains this?
o: Broca's area in the frontal lobe
Broca's area in the temporal lobe
Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe
Wernicke's area in the frontal lobe
w: Two steps: trouble producing speech with comprehension intact points to Broca's area (speech production), and Broca's area lies in the frontal lobe, usually on the left.

n.1: Broca's area is the right area, but it lies in the frontal lobe, not the temporal lobe.
n.2: Wernicke's area handles language comprehension, which is intact here.
n.3: Wernicke's area handles comprehension and lies in the temporal lobe, so both parts are wrong.

q: Signals from the eyes, ears, taste buds and skin pass through one structure in the diencephalon before reaching the cerebral cortex. Which structure is this?
w: The thalamus is the relay station that sends sensory information on to the cerebral cortex. Smell is the one sense not relayed through it first.

n.0: The corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres; it does not relay incoming sensory signals to the cortex.
n.1: The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis and controls the pituitary gland; it is not the main sensory relay.
n.3: The pons is part of the brainstem; it relays signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum and helps regulate breathing.

q: A tumor near the base of the brain disrupts a patient's body temperature control, thirst and pituitary hormone secretion. Which single structure is most likely affected?
w: The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst and water balance and controls the pituitary gland, so one lesion there explains all three problems.

n.0: The thalamus relays sensory information to the cortex; it does not control temperature, thirst or the pituitary.
n.1: The pineal gland secretes melatonin for the sleep-wake cycle.
n.2: The medulla oblongata controls heart rate, breathing and blood pressure, not thirst or pituitary secretion.

q: An injury cuts the ventral (anterior) roots of several spinal nerves in the lower back but leaves the dorsal roots intact. Which result is expected in the areas these nerves supply?
o: Loss of sensation with muscle strength preserved
Loss of both sensation and muscle strength
Loss of pain sensation with touch preserved
w: Two steps: the ventral root carries motor fibers out to muscles, while the dorsal root carries sensory fibers in. Cutting only the ventral roots causes weakness but spares sensation.

n.0: This pattern fits damage to the dorsal (sensory) roots, which are intact here.
n.1: Sensation travels in the dorsal roots, which are intact, so sensation is preserved.
n.2: Both pain and touch enter through the intact dorsal roots, so neither is lost.

q: When asked to stick out his tongue, a patient cannot move it normally, although his taste and facial expressions are intact. Which cranial nerve is most likely damaged?
w: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) controls tongue movement.

n.0: The facial nerve controls facial expression and taste on the front of the tongue, both intact here.
n.2: The trigeminal nerve carries face sensation and controls chewing, not tongue movement.
n.3: Despite its name, CN IX is not the motor nerve of the tongue; tongue movement is controlled by CN XII.

q: Tapping the patellar tendon makes the leg kick forward, while stepping on a tack makes the foot pull away. How does the patellar reflex differ from this withdrawal reflex?
o: It depends on conscious awareness in the cerebral cortex
It has no interneuron between the sensory and motor neurons
It uses an interneuron, while the withdrawal reflex does not
It is processed in the cerebellum before the motor response
w: The patellar (knee-jerk) reflex is monosynaptic: the sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron in the spinal cord. Withdrawal reflexes use interneurons.

n.0: Reflexes are rapid and involuntary; the spinal cord processes them before the brain is aware.
n.2: This reverses the two: withdrawal reflexes use interneurons, and the patellar reflex does not.
n.3: Both reflexes are processed in the spinal cord; the cerebellum is not part of the reflex arc.

q: Which photoreceptors are concentrated in the fovea centralis of the retina and provide color vision and sharp detail in bright light?
w: Cones detect color and fine detail in bright light and are concentrated in the fovea centralis.

n.1: Hair cells are the sensory receptors of the cochlea and inner ear, not the retina.
n.2: Rods work in dim light, give black-and-white vision and serve peripheral vision; they are not concentrated in the fovea.
n.3: Bipolar neurons in the retina pass signals along, but they are not the photoreceptors that detect light.

q: Light passes through several structures on its way to the retina. Which structure does it pass through just before entering the vitreous humor?
w: The light path is cornea, aqueous humor, pupil, lens, vitreous humor, then retina. The lens lies directly in front of the vitreous humor and focuses the light.

n.1: Aqueous humor fills the front of the eye ahead of the lens; the lens separates it from the vitreous humor.
n.2: The cornea is the first structure light crosses, at the very front of the eye.
n.3: The pupil comes before the lens: light passes through the pupil, then the lens, then the vitreous humor.

q: During an airplane's descent, swallowing helps relieve the pressure in Keisha's ears. Which structure connects the middle ear to the pharynx and equalizes this pressure?
w: The auditory (Eustachian) tube connects the middle ear to the pharynx; opening it, for example by swallowing, equalizes pressure on both sides of the eardrum.

n.0: The semicircular canals are inner ear structures for balance.
n.1: The tympanic membrane separates the outer ear from the middle ear; it is the structure the pressure acts on, not a passage to the pharynx.
n.3: The external auditory canal leads from the auricle to the eardrum; it does not connect to the pharynx.

q: Each eye has a small blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina at the optic disc. Why does no image form at this point?
o: It contains rods but no cones
It contains cones but no rods
It is covered by the opaque sclera
w: The optic disc has no photoreceptors (no rods or cones), so light falling on it cannot be detected.

n.1: A region with rods would still detect light in black and white; the optic disc has neither rods nor cones.
n.2: Cones without rods describes the fovea centralis, the point of sharpest vision; the optic disc has neither rods nor cones.
n.3: The sclera is the white outer layer of the eyeball; it does not cover the inner surface of the retina.

q: Spinning rapidly on an office chair leaves Tomás dizzy. Which structures contain the receptors that detect the rotation of his head?
w: The semicircular canals of the inner ear contain the hair-cell receptors that detect rotation of the head. Together with the vestibule they sense balance, and their signals travel on CN VIII.

n.0: The auditory tube equalizes pressure in the middle ear; it does not sense movement.
n.1: The cochlea and its organ of Corti detect sound for hearing, not head rotation.
n.2: The cerebellum uses balance signals to coordinate movement and posture, but it has no receptors; rotation is detected in the semicircular canals.

q: When Priya looks up from her phone to a distant sign, the shape of her lens changes to keep the image focused on the retina. Which structures change the lens shape?
o: Muscles moved by the abducens nerve
w: The ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens so it can focus light from near or distant objects on the retina.

n.0: The choroid is the vascular layer of the eye; it does not change the shape of the lens.
n.1: The muscles of the iris change pupil size, not lens shape.
n.3: The abducens nerve (CN VI) moves the eyeball laterally; it does not focus the lens.

q: A child's ear infection leaves fluid behind the tympanic membrane, so the ossicles cannot vibrate freely. Where is the problem, and which step of hearing is impaired?
o: Outer ear; collecting sound waves into the canal
Middle ear; passing vibrations to the oval window
Middle ear; converting vibrations to nerve impulses
Inner ear; converting vibrations to nerve impulses
w: Two steps: the space behind the tympanic membrane that holds the ossicles is the middle ear, and the ossicles pass vibrations from the eardrum to the oval window. Fluid there weakens that transmission.

n.0: The outer ear (auricle and canal) lies in front of the tympanic membrane, not behind it.
n.2: The location is right, but nerve impulses are generated by hair cells in the cochlea, not in the middle ear.
n.3: Converting vibrations to nerve impulses happens in the cochlea of the inner ear, but the fluid and ossicles are in the middle ear.

q: Which cranial nerve carries visual signals away from the retina, and which lobe of the cerebrum processes these signals?
w: Two steps: the optic nerve (CN II) carries visual signals from the retina, and vision is processed in the occipital lobe.

n.0: CN III is a motor nerve to the eye, and the parietal lobe processes touch and body position.
n.1: The occipital lobe is right, but CN III moves the eye and constricts the pupil; it does not carry visual signals.
n.3: The nerve is right, but the temporal lobe processes hearing, not vision.

q: Which special sense sends its signals to the cerebral cortex without first being relayed through the thalamus?
w: Smell (olfaction) is the one sense whose signals are not relayed through the thalamus before reaching the cortex.

n.0: Hearing signals pass through the thalamus before reaching the auditory cortex.
n.2: Balance signals are also relayed through the thalamus; smell is the exception.
n.3: Taste signals are relayed through the thalamus on their way to the cortex.

q: Small glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid secrete a hormone that raises blood calcium. Which choice names the glands and the hormone?
w: The parathyroid glands, usually four on the back of the thyroid, secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), which raises blood calcium by releasing it from bone, keeping it in the kidneys and activating vitamin D.

n.0: The thymus, in the mediastinum, secretes thymosin for T-cell maturation; it does not regulate calcium.
n.1: Thyroid C (parafollicular) cells secrete calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium; they are part of the thyroid itself.
n.3: The glands are right, but calcitonin comes from the thyroid and lowers calcium; the parathyroids secrete PTH.

q: ADH and oxytocin enter the bloodstream from the posterior pituitary gland. Where are these two hormones synthesized?
w: ADH and oxytocin are made by the hypothalamus and transported to the posterior pituitary, which stores and releases them.

n.0: The posterior pituitary stores and releases ADH and oxytocin, but it does not make them.
n.1: The adrenal cortex makes aldosterone and cortisol, not ADH or oxytocin.
n.3: The anterior pituitary makes its own hormones, such as GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin.

q: A night-shift nurse finds that her normal sleep-wake rhythm is disrupted. Which gland and hormone normally regulate this rhythm, with secretion rising in darkness?
w: The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which rises in darkness and regulates the sleep-wake (circadian) rhythm.

n.0: The pineal gland is right, but cortisol is made by the adrenal cortex.
n.1: The anterior pituitary makes ACTH, not cortisol (adrenal cortex) or melatonin (pineal gland).
n.3: Melatonin comes from the pineal gland, not the anterior pituitary.

q: Seconds after a near-miss on the freeway, Andre's heart races and his hands shake. Which hormone and source produce this short-term stress response?
w: The adrenal medulla (inner region) releases epinephrine and norepinephrine for the short-term, fight-or-flight stress response.

n.0: Epinephrine is made by the adrenal medulla; the adrenal cortex makes aldosterone, cortisol and small amounts of androgens.
n.1: Norepinephrine is released by the adrenal medulla, not the adrenal cortex.
n.3: Cortisol is made by the adrenal cortex and drives the long-term stress response.

q: Which hormone is produced by the anterior pituitary gland and stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete cortisol?
w: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the anterior pituitary stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol.

n.0: GHRH is a hypothalamic releasing hormone that acts on the anterior pituitary to promote growth hormone release, not on the adrenal cortex.
n.1: CRH is a releasing hormone made by the hypothalamus; it acts on the anterior pituitary, not directly on the adrenal cortex.
n.2: TSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the thyroid, not the adrenal cortex.

q: Glucagon is a peptide hormone, and cortisol is a steroid hormone. Which statement correctly compares where each binds its receptor on or in a target cell?
o: Glucagon binds an intracellular receptor; cortisol binds a surface receptor
Both bind surface receptors and act through second messengers such as cAMP
Glucagon binds a surface receptor; cortisol binds an intracellular receptor
Both cross the membrane and bind receptors that change gene expression
w: Two steps: peptide hormones such as glucagon are water-soluble, so they bind cell-membrane receptors and act through second messengers. Steroid hormones such as cortisol are lipid-soluble, so they cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors.

n.0: This reverses the two: peptides bind surface receptors and steroids bind intracellular receptors.
n.1: This fits glucagon, but cortisol is a steroid that binds an intracellular receptor.
n.3: This fits cortisol, but glucagon is water-soluble and cannot cross the membrane; it binds a surface receptor.

q: Besides T3 and T4, the thyroid gland secretes a third hormone from its parafollicular (C) cells. Which hormone is it, and what does it do?
o: Parathyroid hormone; it raises blood calcium
w: The parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid secrete calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium by favoring bone deposition and reducing osteoclast activity.

n.1: The hormone is right, but calcitonin lowers blood calcium; PTH raises it.
n.2: Thymosin is made by the thymus, not by the thyroid gland.
n.3: Parathyroid hormone is made by the parathyroid glands on the back of the thyroid, not by thyroid C cells.

q: A patient has intense thirst and passes very large volumes of dilute urine, but his blood glucose is normal. A deficiency of which hormone, from which gland, best explains this?
o: Aldosterone released from the adrenal medulla
Insulin released from the pancreatic beta cells
ADH released from the anterior pituitary
ADH released from the posterior pituitary
w: Two steps: large volumes of dilute urine with normal glucose is diabetes insipidus, a deficiency of ADH, and ADH is released from the posterior pituitary.

n.0: Aldosterone is made by the adrenal cortex, not the medulla, and diabetes insipidus is a lack of ADH.
n.1: Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus with high blood glucose, but this patient's glucose is normal.
n.2: The hormone is right, but ADH is released from the posterior pituitary, not the anterior pituitary.

q: A patient has lost weight without dieting, feels hot in cool rooms, has a rapid heart rate and has bulging eyes. Excess secretion of which hormones best explains these findings?
o: T3 and T4 from the thyroid gland
Growth hormone from the anterior pituitary
w: T3 and T4 raise metabolic rate and heat production. Excess, as in Graves' disease, causes weight loss, heat intolerance, a fast heart rate and bulging eyes (exophthalmos).

n.1: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium; it does not raise metabolic rate or heat production.
n.2: Excess cortisol causes Cushing's syndrome; heat intolerance, weight loss and bulging eyes point to excess thyroid hormone.
n.3: Excess growth hormone causes gigantism or acromegaly, not this picture of a raised metabolic rate.

q: Over several years, a 34-year-old woman's hands, feet and jaw gradually enlarge, long after her growth plates have closed. Which hormone is in excess, and what is the condition called?
w: Two steps: enlargement of hands, feet and jaw points to excess growth hormone, and excess GH after the growth plates close is acromegaly.

n.0: Cushing's syndrome is excess cortisol and does not cause enlargement of the hands, feet and jaw.
n.1: Gigantism is excess GH before the growth plates close; hers have already closed.
n.2: Gigantism is excess growth hormone before the growth plates close; excess thyroxine raises metabolic rate instead, and her growth plates have closed.

q: A rise in blood volume triggers a hormone that makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, lowering blood pressure. Which hormone and source are correct?
w: When high blood volume stretches the atria, atrial cells release ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide), which makes the kidneys excrete Na⁺ and water, lowering blood volume and pressure.

n.0: ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb water and reduces urine output; it is released when the body needs to keep water.
n.1: Renin is released by the juxtaglomerular cells when blood pressure is low and leads to aldosterone release, which raises blood pressure.
n.3: Aldosterone does the opposite: it makes the kidneys reabsorb Na⁺ (water follows), raising blood volume.

q: Which gland and hormone promote the maturation of T lymphocytes?
w: The thymus, in the mediastinum behind the sternum, secretes thymosin, which promotes the maturation of T cells. The thymus is largest in childhood.

n.0: The thyroid secretes T3 and T4, which raise metabolic rate; the similar name is the trap.
n.1: Calcitonin from the thyroid lowers blood calcium; it has no role in T-cell maturation.
n.2: The gland is right, but thyroxine comes from the thyroid; the thymus secretes thymosin.

q: Shortly after Jamal eats a large pasta dinner, his blood glucose rises. Which hormone does his pancreas release in response, and from which cells?
w: High blood glucose after a meal triggers the beta cells of the pancreatic islets to release insulin, which lowers glucose by moving it into cells and storing it as glycogen.

n.0: Glucagon raises blood glucose, so it is released when glucose is low, not after a meal.
n.2: Insulin is the right hormone, but it comes from beta cells; alpha cells make glucagon.
n.3: Glucagon raises blood glucose and is made by alpha cells, so both parts are wrong.

q: A lab result shows that a patient's blood calcium is below normal. Which hormone responds by stimulating osteoclasts to release calcium from bone?
w: Low blood calcium triggers the parathyroid glands to release PTH, which raises calcium by stimulating osteoclasts, increasing kidney reabsorption of calcium and activating vitamin D.

n.0: TSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the thyroid to release T3 and T4; it does not regulate calcium.
n.1: Calcitonin is released when calcium is high and lowers it by reducing osteoclast activity.
n.2: Aldosterone controls Na⁺ and K⁺ handling by the kidneys, not blood calcium.

q: After several hours of hiking without water, Grace becomes dehydrated and her ADH secretion rises. How does this change the urine her kidneys produce?
o: Smaller volume of more dilute urine
Smaller volume of more concentrated urine
Larger volume of urine containing more sodium
Larger volume of more dilute urine
w: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) makes the collecting ducts reabsorb more water, so the kidneys produce a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

n.0: Reabsorbing more water leaves the remaining urine more concentrated, not more dilute.
n.2: ADH reduces urine volume; increased sodium and water loss is the effect of ANP from the heart.
n.3: This is the effect of low ADH; ADH is anti-diuretic, so it reduces urine output.

q: In the thyroid axis, rising blood levels of T3 and T4 reduce the release of TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH from the anterior pituitary. What type of control is this?
w: The end product (T3 and T4) switches off the signals that produced it, reversing the change. That is negative feedback, the way most hormone levels are controlled.

n.1: Positive feedback amplifies a change until an end event, as oxytocin does in labor; here the change is being reversed.
n.2: The signals in this loop travel as hormones in the blood, not along nerves.
n.3: Antagonistic control means two hormones with opposite effects, such as insulin and glucagon; this is one hormone suppressing its own signals.

q: Between meals, Lena's blood glucose falls below its set point. Which hormone responds, and by which process does her liver raise blood glucose?
o: Glucagon; storage of glucose as glycogen (glycogenesis)
Insulin; storage of glucose as glycogen (glycogenesis)
w: Two steps: low blood glucose triggers the alpha cells to release glucagon, and glucagon makes the liver break down stored glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis), raising blood glucose.

n.0: Insulin lowers blood glucose and is released after meals, not when glucose is low.
n.1: Glucagon is the right hormone, but storing glucose as glycogen lowers blood glucose; that is an effect of insulin.
n.2: Both parts lower blood glucose: insulin is released after meals and promotes glycogenesis, the opposite of what low glucose requires.

q: When blood pressure and blood volume fall, the adrenal cortex increases its secretion of aldosterone. Which effect of aldosterone on the kidneys helps restore blood volume?
o: Reabsorbing Na⁺ (water follows) and excreting K⁺
Reabsorbing K⁺ (water follows) and excreting Na⁺
Excreting Na⁺ and water to reduce the workload on the heart
Reabsorbing Ca²⁺ in the distal tubule to raise blood volume
w: Aldosterone makes the kidneys reabsorb Na⁺, with water following by osmosis, and excrete K⁺. The retained water raises blood volume and blood pressure.

n.1: This reverses the ions: aldosterone causes Na⁺ retention and K⁺ excretion.
n.2: Excreting Na⁺ and water lowers blood volume; that is the action of ANP from the heart.
n.3: Increasing Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the distal tubule is an action of PTH and controls blood calcium, not blood volume.

q: During weeks of ongoing stress before final exams, which hormone sustains Mei's long-term stress response by raising blood glucose and suppressing inflammation?
w: Cortisol, a glucocorticoid from the adrenal cortex, drives the long-term stress response: it raises blood glucose by gluconeogenesis, is anti-inflammatory and suppresses immunity.

n.1: Cortisol is the right hormone, but it comes from the adrenal cortex, not the medulla.
n.2: Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla drives the short-term, fight-or-flight response, not weeks of sustained stress.
n.3: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex controls Na⁺ and K⁺ and blood volume, not glucose or inflammation.

q: A 45-year-old patient with obesity has high blood glucose even though his pancreas still produces insulin. Which description best fits his condition?
o: Type 1 diabetes mellitus caused by beta-cell destruction
Type 2 diabetes mellitus caused by insulin resistance
Diabetes insipidus caused by a lack of ADH
Type 1 diabetes mellitus caused by insulin resistance
w: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is mainly insulin resistance (with a relative deficiency) and is linked to obesity and inactivity; insulin is still produced.

n.0: Beta-cell destruction leaves no insulin, but this patient still produces insulin.
n.2: Diabetes insipidus is an ADH problem causing dilute urine; it does not raise blood glucose.
n.3: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of beta cells; insulin resistance defines type 2.

q: Alcohol inhibits the secretion of ADH. Compared with a well-hydrated person who has not been drinking, what would be expected in a person who has had several alcoholic drinks?
o: Less water reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so more dilute urine
Less water reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, so less urine
More water reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so less urine
More Na⁺ reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so more concentrated urine
w: Two steps: ADH acts on the collecting ducts to increase water reabsorption, so less ADH means less water is reabsorbed there and a larger volume of more dilute urine is produced.

n.1: ADH acts on the collecting ducts, not the proximal tubule, and reabsorbing less water produces more urine, not less.
n.2: This is the effect of more ADH; alcohol lowers ADH.
n.3: Na⁺ reabsorption is controlled by aldosterone, and lower ADH makes urine more dilute, not more concentrated.

q: An autoimmune process destroys a patient's adrenal cortex but spares the adrenal medulla. Which hormone deficiencies, and which effect, would be expected?
o: Low epinephrine and norepinephrine; a weaker fight-or-flight response
Low cortisol and aldosterone; high blood glucose from gluconeogenesis
Low cortisol and aldosterone; low blood pressure from Na⁺ loss
Low cortisol and aldosterone; high blood pressure from Na⁺ retention
w: Two steps: the adrenal cortex makes cortisol and aldosterone, so both fall (Addison's disease). Without aldosterone the kidneys lose Na⁺ and the water that follows it, so blood volume and blood pressure fall.

n.0: Epinephrine and norepinephrine come from the adrenal medulla, which is spared.
n.1: The deficiencies are right, but cortisol raises blood glucose by gluconeogenesis, so losing it tends to lower glucose rather than raise it.
n.3: The deficiencies are right, but aldosterone causes Na⁺ retention, so its loss leads to Na⁺ loss and lower blood pressure.

q: A person's diet lacks iodine, so the thyroid makes too little T3 and T4. Through negative feedback, what happens to TSH secretion and the thyroid gland?
o: TSH falls, and the thyroid enlarges
TSH rises, and the thyroid enlarges
TSH falls, and the thyroid shrinks
TSH rises, and the thyroid shrinks
w: Low T3 and T4 remove the negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, so TRH and TSH rise. Constant TSH stimulation enlarges the thyroid, producing a goiter.

n.0: Falling TSH would leave the thyroid unstimulated; the goiter forms because TSH is high.
n.2: TSH falls when T3 and T4 are high; here they are low, so the brake on TSH is released.
n.3: TSH does rise, but continuous TSH stimulation makes the gland grow, not shrink.

q: In the stress axis, the hypothalamus, anterior pituitary and adrenal cortex signal in sequence. Which hormone sequence ends in cortisol release?
w: The hypothalamus releases CRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release ACTH, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete cortisol. Rising cortisol then inhibits CRH and ACTH release (negative feedback).

n.0: TSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the thyroid, not the adrenal cortex.
n.1: The order is reversed: CRH from the hypothalamus comes first and triggers ACTH release.
n.3: GHRH triggers growth hormone release; CRH is the hypothalamic hormone of the stress axis.
